why_how.text: More than ninety percent of highway crashes trace back to the driver, so your state of mind matters as much as your skills.
Strong emotions and worries can make anyone temporarily accident-prone.

scenario.text: Chris has just had a heated argument at home and is still furious when it is time to drive to work.

reasoning.text: The manual says someone who just had a violent argument or is angry needs time to cool off, and an angry driver should let another person drive.

result.text: Chris waits to calm down, or asks a family member to drive instead of venting the anger on the road.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking that once you have mastered the basic skills, you know all you need to drive well.

correction.text: Basic skills are not enough; a good driver keeps learning the finer points and the conditions that affect driving.

memory_support.text: Calm mind, full attention, shared road.

prompt.text: A friend feels nervous and frightened but wants to drive the group home. What does the manual advise?

rationale.text: When you feel worried, ill, nervous, frightened, angry or depressed, the manual's advice is to hand the driving to someone else.

lines.text: Most crashes trace to the driver.

narration.text: This chapter is about the driver, and it opens with a striking fact. According to crash records, more than ninety percent of highway crashes trace back to the driver: error, missing knowledge, inattention, physical or mental condition, a poor attitude or faulty judgment. That means the most important safety feature in any car is the person behind the wheel. In this lesson you will look at how worries and strong emotions affect driving, what a mature and socially responsible driver looks like, and why concentration has to be complete every moment you drive.

Learning to steer, brake and park is only the beginning. Basic skills are not enough to make a good driver. After mastering them, you must keep learning the finer points of driving and the physical and mental conditions that affect it. Think of it the way professional drivers do: the basics get you on the road, but understanding how fatigue, emotions, alcohol and distraction change your driving is what keeps you safe over the years. The rest of this chapter is about exactly those conditions, starting with your state of mind. A calm, focused mind is the best safety feature a car can have.

lines.text: Cool off after anger or grief.

narration.text: Family troubles, quarrels, money worries, a serious illness at home, personal fears or overconfidence can make you temporarily accident-prone, because a preoccupied mind cannot stay alert enough to drive safely. Strong emotions work the same way. Someone who has just had a violent argument, or who is angry or grieving, needs time to cool off before driving, since venting emotions behind the wheel is very poor judgment. And when you feel worried, ill, nervous, frightened, angry or depressed, the manual's advice is simple: let another person drive.

lines.text: Act from every road user's view.

narration.text: A well-adjusted driver understands that traffic means sharing the road fairly, and acts not just from a personal point of view but from the point of view of every road user. The manual calls that social responsibility. Good driving attitudes and sound actions show mental and emotional maturity, and that maturity matters for younger and older drivers alike. Behind the wheel, people quickly show whether they are courteous and reliable or thoughtless and pushy. Choosing to share the road fairly is a decision every driver can make on every trip.

lines.text: Handing over the keys is for worry or fear.

narration.text: Here is where learners mix things up. The manual gives two pieces of advice that sound alike. After a violent argument, or when angry or grieving, you need time to cool off before you drive. But when you feel worried, ill, nervous, frightened, angry or depressed, the advice is to let another person drive. Both come from the same idea, that a preoccupied mind cannot stay alert. So if a question describes someone who is upset or frightened and asks what to do, waiting to calm down or handing the keys to someone else are the safe answers. A calm, focused mind is the best safety feature a car can have.

lines.text: Nervous and frightened: what to do?

narration.text: Here is a quick check: a friend feels nervous and frightened but wants to drive the group home. What does the manual advise? Make your choice, then compare. The answer is to let another person drive. When you feel worried, ill, nervous, frightened, angry or depressed, the manual's advice is to hand the driving to someone else, because a preoccupied mind cannot stay alert enough to drive safely. Driving slowly or carefully while upset is not the advice. The safest choice is for someone calm and alert to take the wheel. A calm, focused mind is the best safety feature a car can have.

Concentration is among the most important parts of safe driving. The driver's seat is no place for daydreaming, window shopping, sightseeing or distracting talk. Driving is a full-time job, and poor concentration dulls your observation enough to cause crashes that could have been avoided. Many drivers who survive crashes say they do not know what happened, which is often a sign that their attention was somewhere else. So keep your mind on the road and your eyes on the traffic around you, from the moment you start the engine until you park.

why_how.text: A phone call or a text pulls attention away from the full-time job of driving.

scenario.text: Jamie's phone buzzes with a text while she is driving in heavy traffic.

reasoning.text: Alabama bans writing, sending or reading texts while operating a vehicle, and the manual says to avoid phone use in heavy traffic and pull off to finish a conversation.

result.text: Jamie leaves the text unread until she is parked, avoiding a fine and two points on her record.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking it is fine to read a text as long as you do not write one.

correction.text: The law bans using a wireless device to write, send or read texts, instant messages or e-mail while operating a vehicle.

prompt.text: A driver is caught texting for the second time. What fine and points does the manual list?

answer.text: A fifty-dollar fine and two points.

rationale.text: The second texting offense is fifty dollars, and every texting offense adds a two-point violation.

narration.text: Cell phones are part of daily life, but behind the wheel they compete with the full-time job of driving. This lesson covers two things. First, the precautions the manual lists if you do use a phone while driving, all built around one idea: your first responsibility is still driving the vehicle. Second, Alabama's ban on texting while operating a motor vehicle, which goes further than precautions and forbids the activity outright. You will also learn the fines and points that come with texting violations, so you know exactly what is at stake.

lines.text: Size up traffic; know your keypad.
Call when stopped or by a passenger.

narration.text: If you use a cell phone while driving, your first responsibility is still driving the vehicle. Before making a call, size up the traffic, and know your keypad well enough to use speed dial where you can. Better still, make calls while stopped, or let a passenger place them for you. Keep the phone within easy reach, so you are not stretching for it, and use a speaker phone or a hands-free device. Each of these steps reduces the time your eyes and hands spend on the phone instead of on the road. Driving stays your first job every time the phone rings.

lines.text: Pull off to dial or finish.

narration.text: Some calls should wait. Steer clear of intense, emotional or complicated conversations while driving, because they pull your mind away from the road just as strong emotions do. Avoid phone talk in heavy traffic or bad weather, when driving needs all your attention. And if you need to dial or finish a conversation, pull off the road to do it. The pattern is clear: the more demanding the call or the driving conditions, the more important it is to stop, or to let the call wait until you are parked somewhere safe. Driving stays your first job every time the phone rings.

lines.text: Fines rise; two points each time.

narration.text: While operating a motor vehicle in Alabama, you may not use a wireless device to write, send or read texts, instant messages or e-mail. Reading counts, not only writing and sending. The manual lists texting fines of twenty-five dollars for a first offense, fifty dollars for a second, and seventy-five dollars for a third or later offense. On top of the fine, every texting offense also adds a two-point violation to the offender's driving record. So a single glance at a message can cost you both money and points. Driving stays your first job every time the phone rings.

Here is a trap with the texting penalties. The fines climb with each offense: twenty-five dollars, then fifty, then seventy-five for a third or later offense. But the points do not climb. Every texting offense adds the same two-point violation to the driving record, whether it is the first or the fifth. A question might suggest the points double or triple along with the fine; that is not what the manual says. Keep the two pieces separate in your mind: the money rises, and the two points arrive every single time. Driving stays your first job every time the phone rings.

lines.text: Second texting offense: fine and points?

narration.text: Here is a quick check: a driver is caught texting for the second time. What fine and points does the manual list? Settle on your answer, then compare. The answer is a fifty-dollar fine and two points. The first offense is twenty-five dollars and the third or later is seventy-five dollars, while every offense carries the same two-point violation. If you guessed four points for a second offense, remember that the points do not grow. Only the fine changes as the offenses add up. Driving stays your first job every time the phone rings. A message can always wait until you are parked.

lines.text: No texting; fines rise, two points each.

narration.text: To sum up, if you use a cell phone while driving, your first responsibility is still driving. Size up traffic before calling, use speed dial, call while stopped or let a passenger call, keep the phone within reach, and use a speaker or hands-free device. Avoid intense or complicated calls, heavy traffic and bad weather, and pull off to dial or finish a conversation. Texting is banned outright: you may not write, send or read texts, instant messages or e-mail while operating a vehicle. Fines run twenty-five, fifty and seventy-five dollars, and every offense adds two points.

why_how.text: Drowsiness is one of the biggest dangers of interstate driving, so knowing when to stop can save your life.

scenario.text: Sam has been driving on the interstate for two hours and starts to feel drowsy.

reasoning.text: The manual says to stop instead of fighting drowsiness and to take a break every one hundred miles or two hours.

result.text: Sam leaves at the first rest stop, walks and stretches, and naps if truly sleepy before going on.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking a stay-awake drug is a safe way to push through a long drive.

correction.text: Stay-awake drugs are likely to make your driving more dangerous; a truly sleepy driver should get off the highway and nap.

memory_support.text: Drowsy means stop, sleepy means nap.

prompt.text: How often does the manual suggest taking a break on a long trip?

answer.text: Every one hundred miles or every two hours.

rationale.text: Regular breaks every one hundred miles or two hours, with a walk and a stretch, help keep fatigue away.

narration.text: Long drives bring their own dangers, and drowsiness is one of the biggest dangers of interstate driving. In this lesson you will learn what to do the moment you feel drowsy, how coffee and naps fit in, why stay-awake drugs are a bad idea, and how often to take a break. Then we will look at highway hypnosis, a drowsy, unaware state caused by the monotony of expressway driving, and the simple eye habits that help you fight it. These are habits you can start on your very first long trip. Rest is the only real cure for drowsiness. Stopping early is always safer than pushing on.

lines.text: Leave at the first rest stop.

narration.text: Stop driving as soon as you feel drowsy instead of trying to fight it, and leave the highway at the first rest stop or service area. A driver who is only getting tired may be revived by coffee and some stretching. But a driver who is truly sleepy should get off the highway and take a nap. Drowsiness is one of the biggest dangers of interstate driving, and stay-awake drugs are likely to make your driving more dangerous, not less. So the safe responses are stopping, resting and sleeping, not pushing on. Rest is the only real cure for drowsiness.

lines.text: Break every hundred miles or two hours.

narration.text: Plan rest into long drives. Take a regular break every one hundred miles or every two hours, getting out of the car to walk, stretch and relax. Before a long trip, it is a good idea to take a nap, so you start out rested rather than already tired. These habits work together. A nap before you leave delays fatigue, and regular breaks keep it from building up. If you still feel drowsy despite them, the rule from the last slide applies: stop and rest rather than trying to fight it on the road. Rest is the only real cure for drowsiness. Stopping early is always safer than pushing on.

lines.text: Tired: coffee and a stretch may help.

narration.text: Here is the trap. Many drivers treat all fatigue the same and reach for coffee or a stay-awake pill. The manual draws a line. A driver who is only getting tired may get by with coffee and some stretching. But a truly sleepy driver must leave the highway and nap, because coffee will not fix real sleepiness. And drugs to stay awake are never the answer, since they are likely to make driving more dangerous. When a question describes a driver who is nodding off, the right answer is to stop and sleep. Rest is the only real cure for drowsiness. Stopping early is always safer than pushing on.

Expressway drivers are prone to highway hypnosis, which is drowsiness or unawareness caused by monotony. The sound of the wind, the tires on the pavement and the steady hum of the engine can lull you into a trance-like state where you are driving without really paying attention. To fight highway hypnosis, keep moving your eyes from one area of the roadway to another, and focus on objects near and far, left and right. Reading highway signs can also keep you alert. Active eyes keep an active mind. Rest is the only real cure for drowsiness. Stopping early is always safer than pushing on.

lines.text: How often should you take a break?

narration.text: Here is a quick check: how often does the manual suggest taking a break on a long trip? Decide on your answer first. The answer is every one hundred miles or every two hours. On each break, get out of the car to walk, stretch and relax. Combine that with a nap before a long trip, and you start rested and stay fresher. If drowsiness still hits between breaks, stop at the first rest stop or service area, and if you are truly sleepy, take a nap before driving any farther. Rest is the only real cure for drowsiness. Stopping early is always safer than pushing on.

lines.text: Stop when drowsy; nap when sleepy.

narration.text: To wrap up, drowsiness is one of the biggest dangers of interstate driving. Stop as soon as you feel drowsy and leave at the first rest stop. Coffee and stretching may help a tired driver, but a truly sleepy driver needs to get off the highway and nap, and stay-awake drugs only add danger. Take a break every one hundred miles or two hours, and nap before a long trip. Fight highway hypnosis by moving your eyes near and far, left and right, and reading highway signs to stay alert. Rest is the only real cure for drowsiness. Stopping early is always safer than pushing on.

why_how.text: Drinking drivers are involved in roughly half of fatal crashes, so understanding alcohol's effects is essential.
Alcohol works in ways people often misunderstand, which leads to dangerous choices.

scenario.text: After two beers, Riley feels lively and thinks a cup of coffee will make it safe to drive.

reasoning.text: The lively feeling is lowered inhibitions, since alcohol is a depressant, and coffee may wake Riley but will not sober him.

result.text: Riley is still impaired and should not drive; only time lets the liver break the alcohol down.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking beer is safer than whiskey or wine.

correction.text: One bottle of beer holds about as much alcohol as a shot of whiskey or a glass of wine, and what counts is how much alcohol reaches the blood.

memory_support.text: Point zero five starts it; only time ends it.

prompt.text: A friend says a cold shower will sober him up before he drives. Is he right?

answer.text: No; it may wake him, but it will not sober him.

rationale.text: Once alcohol is in the blood the liver must break it down over time, so only time sobers a person.

lines.text: Half of fatal crashes involve drinkers.

narration.text: Your physical condition strongly affects your driving, and alcohol, drugs, illness or disability can cause or contribute to crashes. Alcohol deserves special attention. Drinking by drivers is a major contributing factor in traffic crashes, and the manual reports that drinking drivers are involved in roughly fifty percent of fatal crashes each year. In this lesson you will learn how impairment grows with blood alcohol, why a beer counts the same as a shot, what alcohol really does to your body, and why the usual tricks for sobering up do not work.

lines.text: Point zero five impairs most drivers.

narration.text: Research shows that a blood alcohol concentration of point zero five percent already impairs most people's driving to some degree. Impairment grows as blood alcohol concentration rises, and at point zero eight percent every person is definitely impaired. A driver can be impaired before reaching the point of legal intoxication. In other words, there is no safe zone just under the legal limit. The impairment is already there well before you reach it, which is why the safest choice is not to drink at all if you plan to drive. The safest choice is not to drive after drinking.

lines.text: Beer, shot or wine: about the same.
The amount in your blood counts.

narration.text: The manual says one bottle of beer holds about as much alcohol as an average shot of whiskey or a glass of wine, with the same effect on the average driver. Beer, wine or whiskey makes no difference; what counts is how much alcohol reaches the blood. Alcohol can also hit you differently from one time to the next, and a small amount affects you more on an empty stomach than after eating. So counting drinks by type, or assuming beer is mild, is a mistake. Each drink adds roughly the same alcohol to your blood. The safest choice is not to drive after drinking.

Alcohol is a depressant rather than a stimulant. It brings drowsiness, blurred vision and slower reflexes, and it weakens judgment and coordination. People who feel stimulated after drinking are really experiencing lowered inhibitions, which strip away caution and self-control. That is a dangerous combination behind the wheel: slower reactions plus less caution. The manual sums up the reasons not to drink and drive: alcohol dulls judgment, slows reflexes, impairs vision, harms coordination, removes inhibitions, breeds overconfidence and prevents concentration.

lines.text: Impairment starts at point zero five.
The legal limit is point zero eight.

narration.text: Here is a trap. Many people think they are fine as long as they stay under the legal limit. But research puts the start of impairment for most drivers at point zero five percent, below the point zero eight percent level that makes driving unlawful. A driver can be impaired before reaching the point of legal intoxication. So a question that asks whether a driver under the limit can be impaired should be answered yes. The legal limit marks when driving becomes unlawful, not when it becomes dangerous. The safest choice is not to drive after drinking.

lines.text: Coffee or a shower may wake you.

narration.text: Black coffee, food or a cold shower may wake you up, but they will not sober you. Once alcohol is in the bloodstream, the liver must break it down over time before the body eliminates it, and that process cannot be hurried. This is why someone who feels more alert after coffee is still just as impaired. The only cure for alcohol in the blood is time. If you have been drinking, the safe plan is not to drive at all, rather than trying a trick that leaves you awake but still impaired. The safest choice is not to drive after drinking. Alcohol is a depressant, whatever it feels like.

lines.text: Does a cold shower sober you?

narration.text: Here is a quick check: a friend says a cold shower will sober him up before he drives. Is he right? Think it through first. The answer is no. A cold shower, black coffee or food may wake a person up, but they will not sober him. Once alcohol is in the blood, the liver must break it down over time, and only time does that. Feeling more alert is not the same as being less impaired, so your friend should not drive. Remember that impairment can start at point zero five percent, well below the legal limit. The safest choice is not to drive after drinking.

lines.text: Same alcohol per drink; only time sobers.

narration.text: To close, physical condition matters, and drinking drivers are involved in roughly fifty percent of fatal crashes. Impairment begins for most people at point zero five percent, everyone is impaired at point zero eight, and you can be impaired before legal intoxication. A beer, a shot and a glass of wine carry about the same alcohol, and an empty stomach makes a small amount hit harder. Alcohol is a depressant; feeling lively is just lowered inhibitions. Coffee, food or a cold shower will not sober you, because only time lets the liver do its work.

why_how.text: Knowing the limit that applies to you, and what implied consent means, keeps you from losing your license.

scenario.text: Taylor, nineteen, is stopped and tests at point zero three percent blood alcohol.

reasoning.text: Drivers under twenty-one are held to point zero two percent, much lower than the general point zero eight limit.

result.text: Taylor is over the under-twenty-one limit even though an adult would be under the general limit.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking everyone is held to the same point zero eight percent limit.

correction.text: Commercial operators are held to point zero four percent, and drivers under twenty-one and school bus or daycare drivers to point zero two.

memory_support.text: Eight for most, four for commercial, two for young and bus.

prompt.text: What blood alcohol level is unlawful for a commercial vehicle operator?

answer.text: Point zero four percent or more.

rationale.text: Commercial operators are held to point zero four percent, half the general point zero eight limit.

lines.text: The general limit and special limits.

narration.text: This lesson turns from how alcohol affects you to what the law says about it. You will learn the general blood alcohol limit for Alabama drivers, the offenses that cover driving or controlling a vehicle while under the influence, and the much lower limits that apply to commercial drivers, to drivers under twenty-one, and to school bus and daycare drivers. Finally, you will see what Alabama's implied consent law means: that by driving on public highways you have already agreed to chemical testing, and what happens if you refuse a breath test.

lines.text: Point zero eight percent or more.

narration.text: Under Alabama law it is unlawful to drive with a blood alcohol concentration of point zero eight percent or more, or while under the influence of alcohol. State law also forbids driving, or being in actual physical control of a vehicle, while under the influence of alcohol or drugs, or of a drug or an alcohol-drug combination that leaves you unable to drive safely. So the law covers more than a number on a test. Sitting in control of the vehicle counts, and drug or combined impairment counts too, even without a measured alcohol level. Know which limit applies to you before you ever get behind the wheel.

lines.text: Under twenty-one, school bus, daycare: point zero two.

narration.text: Some drivers are held to stricter limits. For commercial vehicle operators, the unlawful blood alcohol level is point zero four percent or more. For persons under twenty-one years of age, it is point zero two percent or more. For school bus and daycare drivers, it is also point zero two percent or more. These lower limits reflect extra responsibility, such as driving large vehicles or carrying children, and the higher risk for young drivers. For a teen driver, even a small amount of alcohol can put you over your limit. Know which limit applies to you before you ever get behind the wheel.

lines.text: Commercial four; young and bus two.

narration.text: Here is the trap. Test questions often give a blood alcohol level and a type of driver, then ask whether the driver is over the limit. The general limit is point zero eight percent, but commercial operators are held to point zero four, and drivers under twenty-one and school bus or daycare drivers are held to point zero two. So a nineteen-year-old at point zero three percent is over the limit, even though an adult at the same level would not be over the general limit. Always identify the driver first, then the limit that applies. Know which limit applies to you before you ever get behind the wheel.

lines.text: Refusing a breath test brings suspension.

narration.text: Under the implied consent law, anyone driving on Alabama's public highways is treated as having agreed to chemical testing of their blood, breath or urine for alcohol content. You do not sign anything; the agreement comes with the act of driving. A driver who has been arrested for DUI and refuses an officer's direction to take a chemical breath test will have the driver license suspended. So refusing a test does not avoid trouble. It brings its own penalty, separate from whatever the test might have shown. Know which limit applies to you before you ever get behind the wheel.

Here is a quick check: what blood alcohol level is unlawful for a commercial vehicle operator? Decide first, then listen. The answer is point zero four percent or more, which is half the general point zero eight percent limit. Drivers under twenty-one and school bus or daycare drivers are held even lower, at point zero two percent. If you answered point zero eight, you gave the general limit for most drivers. Remember to match the limit to the type of driver every time you see one of these questions. Know which limit applies to you before you ever get behind the wheel.

To sum up, it is unlawful to drive with a blood alcohol concentration of point zero eight percent or more, or while under the influence, and being in actual physical control while impaired by alcohol, drugs or both is forbidden too. Commercial operators are held to point zero four percent, while drivers under twenty-one and school bus or daycare drivers are held to point zero two. Driving on Alabama's public highways means you have agreed to chemical testing, and refusing a breath test after a DUI arrest leads to suspension of your license.

why_how.text: The penalties for DUI grow sharply with each conviction, from a suspension to a felony.

scenario.text: Morgan is convicted of DUI for the second time in seven years.

reasoning.text: A second conviction within ten years brings a fine of one thousand one hundred to five thousand one hundred dollars, possible jail, mandatory jail time or community service, and a one-year revocation.

result.text: Morgan loses the license for a year and must serve forty-eight hours in jail or twenty days of community service.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking a first DUI conviction leads to revocation.

correction.text: A first conviction brings a ninety-day suspension; the one-year revocation comes with a second conviction within ten years.

memory_support.text: Ninety days, one year, three years, felony.

prompt.text: A driver is convicted of DUI for the third time. How long is the license revoked?

rationale.text: A third conviction costs the license for three years, while a fourth or later is a felony with a five-year revocation.

narration.text: Driving under the influence carries penalties that climb with every conviction, and this lesson walks you up the ladder one step at a time. You will see the fines, jail terms and license penalties for a first, second, third, and fourth or later conviction. Pay special attention to the license penalties, because they change from a suspension to a revocation and grow longer each time, and to the point where a DUI becomes a felony. These are some of the most serious consequences anywhere in the driver manual. Each conviction is far more costly than the one before.

lines.text: First: fine, possible jail, ninety-day suspension.
Second within ten years: one-year revocation.

narration.text: For a first DUI conviction, the penalty is a fine of six hundred to two thousand one hundred dollars, a jail term of up to one year, or both, and the license is suspended for ninety days. A second conviction within ten years brings a fine of one thousand one hundred to five thousand one hundred dollars, up to one year in jail or both, a mandatory forty-eight hours in jail or twenty days of community service, and a one-year license revocation. Notice the change from a suspension after the first conviction to a revocation after the second. Each conviction is far more costly than the one before.

lines.text: Fourth or later: Class C felony.

narration.text: A third conviction brings a fine of two thousand one hundred to ten thousand one hundred dollars, a three-year license revocation, and up to one year in jail with a mandatory minimum of sixty days that cannot be probated or suspended. A fourth or later conviction is a Class C felony, with fines of four thousand one hundred to ten thousand one hundred dollars, a five-year revocation, and imprisonment of at least one year and one day and no more than ten years. At that point a DUI is treated as a serious crime. Each conviction is far more costly than the one before.

Here is a trap. People often assume that any DUI conviction means revocation. But a first DUI conviction brings a ninety-day suspension, while a second conviction within ten years brings a one-year revocation. Further up the ladder, a third conviction costs the license for three years, and a fourth or later conviction is a felony with a five-year revocation. So match each conviction number to its license penalty: ninety days, one year, three years, five years. Mixing up suspension and revocation is one of the easiest ways to miss a question here.

lines.text: Third DUI: how long without a license?

narration.text: Here is a quick check: a driver is convicted of DUI for the third time. How long is the license revoked? Settle on your answer first. The answer is three years. A third conviction also brings a large fine and up to a year in jail, with a sixty-day minimum that cannot be probated or suspended. A fourth or later conviction is a felony with a five-year revocation. If you answered one year, you were thinking of a second conviction within ten years, and ninety days belongs to a first conviction. Each conviction is far more costly than the one before.

lines.text: Ninety days, one year, three, five.
Fourth or later is a felony.

narration.text: To finish, a first DUI conviction brings a fine, possible jail and a ninety-day suspension. A second within ten years brings a higher fine, possible jail, a mandatory forty-eight hours in jail or twenty days of community service, and a one-year revocation. A third brings a fine up to ten thousand one hundred dollars, a three-year revocation and at least sixty days in jail. A fourth or later is a Class C felony with a five-year revocation and prison from one year and one day up to ten years. Each step is far worse than the last. Each conviction is far more costly than the one before.
